t: Number of Ways to Select Buildings — Counting Alternating Triples
o: We must pick three buildings from a binary string so that consecutive picks alternate types, meaning the selected pattern is exactly "010" or "101". For s = "001101" the six valid index sets are listed in the statement and all reduce to those two patterns. For s = "11100" there is no alternating triple, so the answer is 0. Since $s$ can have length $10^5$, checking all triples ($O(n^3)$) is hopeless, and even enumerating pairs of ends per middle is too slow — we need per-index counting with prefix information.
k: A valid selection is any subsequence equal to "010" or "101", so only the type of the middle building matters.
Fixing the middle building at index i, the number of ways is (count of opposite characters before i) times (count of opposite characters after i).
Everything reduces to running counts of zeros and ones seen so far, giving a constant-space single pass.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute Force Over All Triples
a.i: Enumerate every combination i < j < k and count it when s[j] differs from both s[i] and s[k]. This directly mirrors the definition of a valid selection and is useful to validate faster solutions on small inputs, but it examines roughly $n^3/6$ triples.
s: Loop i from 0 to n-1, j from i+1 to n-1, k from j+1 to n-1.
If s[i] != s[j] and s[j] != s[k], increment ans.
a.t: O(n^3) — all triples are enumerated; far too slow for n = 10^5.

a.n: Approach 2: Multiply Left/Right Opposite Counts per Middle
a.i: Every valid triple has a unique middle building whose neighbors are both of the opposite type. Precompute for each position how many opposite characters lie before it and after it; the product counts exactly the triples centered there, and products never overlap because each triple has one middle. The answer can reach ~$(10^5)^2$, so accumulate in 64 bits.
s: Sweep left to right keeping counts z, o of zeros/ones seen; store left[i] = opposite count before i, then update counts.
Reset counts and sweep right to left to fill right[i] similarly.
Sum left[i] * right[i] over all i.
a.sp: O(n) — two auxiliary arrays of size n.

a.i: Maintain cnt0/cnt1 (zeros/ones so far) plus p01/p10 (number of "01"/"10" subsequences so far). Seeing '1' completes triples of shape "101": add p10 to the answer, then update p01 with cnt0. Symmetrically for '0'. This folds the left/right arrays of Approach 2 into four scalars and processes the string in a single pass.
s: Initialize cnt0 = cnt1 = p01 = p10 = ans = 0.
For ch == '0': p10 += cnt1, ans += p01, cnt0++.
For ch == '1': p01 += cnt0, ans += p10, cnt1++.
a.t: O(n) — a single scan with O(1) work per character.
a.sp: O(1) — four counters and the answer.

w: Lead with the observation that valid selections are exactly subsequences "010"/"101", then present Approach 3 as the optimal solution (Approach 2 is easier to explain and equally fast asymptotically). Pitfalls: counting substrings instead of subsequences, forgetting that the answer needs 64-bit storage (up to ~2.5 * 10^9), and updating pair counts before using them for triples in Approach 3 — order matters within each branch. Edge cases include strings of all identical characters (answer 0). Follow-ups: generalize to selecting k buildings, or count selections mod 10^9+7 when answers grow larger.
